title: How to read sugar, fat, and sodium on a Nutrition Facts label

seo.title: How to read sugar, fat, and sodium on a food label
seo.meta_description: Learn how to compare saturated fat, sodium, total and added sugars, serving size, and % Daily Value on U.S. Nutrition Facts labels.
seo.search_intent: Learn how to interpret saturated fat, sodium, total sugar, added sugar, serving size, and % Daily Value on U.S. Nutrition Facts labels.

excerpt: A Nutrition Facts label becomes much easier once you separate three questions: what is in one serving, how that serving compares with a daily reference, and how many servings you actually eat.
content_html:
A Nutrition Facts label is not just a scoreboard of “good” and “bad” numbers. It answers three different questions: what is in one labeled serving, how that amount compares with a Daily Value, and how much you actually eat. Confusing those questions is where most label-reading mistakes begin.

Start with serving size

In the United States, the calories and nutrient amounts on the Nutrition Facts panel refer to the labeled serving. If one serving lists 280 calories and you eat two servings, the total becomes 560 calories and each listed nutrient amount doubles as well.

FDA’s sample label, for example, shows 850 mg sodium in one serving and 1,700 mg in two servings. The food did not change; the amount eaten did.

Total sugars and added sugars are not the same thing

Total Sugars includes naturally occurring sugars plus any sugars added during processing. Milk lactose and fruit sugars can therefore appear in Total Sugars even when no table sugar was added.

Added Sugars is listed separately underneath. If a yogurt contains 15 g Total Sugars and “Includes 7 g Added Sugars,” then roughly 8 g is naturally occurring and 7 g was added.

Look at saturated fat, not just total fat

Two foods can contain the same total fat but very different saturated fat. If product A has 15 g total fat and 2 g saturated fat while product B has 15 g total fat and 8 g saturated fat, total fat alone hides a 6 g difference in saturated fat.

FDA’s Daily Value for saturated fat is 20 g on a 2,000-calorie reference diet. It is a “less than” target, not a goal to hit.

Sodium needs both milligrams and context

The U.S. label lists sodium, not salt. FDA’s Daily Value is 2,300 mg sodium. One serving with 575 mg therefore supplies 25% DV; two servings would provide 1,150 mg, or 50% DV.

If you are comparing with a European label that lists salt instead, the rough conversion is 1 g sodium ≈ 2.5 g salt.

Use the 5% and 20% DV shortcut

FDA describes 5% DV or less per serving as low and 20% DV or more as high. This is especially useful for nutrients such as saturated fat, sodium, added sugars, fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, and potassium.

For example, 23% DV saturated fat is high for one serving; 4% DV is low. The shortcut does not make the entire food healthy or unhealthy—it tells you how much that serving contributes for that nutrient.

Added sugar has a Daily Value; total sugar does not

FDA sets the Daily Value for Added Sugars at 50 g on a 2,000-calorie diet. Total Sugars does not have a %DV because there is no established Daily Value for total sugar.

That distinction prevents a plain dairy food or fruit-containing product from being treated exactly like a product with the same grams of sugar added during processing.

A 20-second label routine

First, check serving size and servings per container. Second, scan saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars. Third, look at fiber and other nutrients relevant to your goal. Fourth, multiply the numbers if your actual portion differs from the labeled serving.

The useful takeaway

The label is most useful when you compare like with like and connect the listed serving with the amount you actually eat. Total fat is not the same as saturated fat, Total Sugars is not the same as Added Sugars, and a %DV describes one nutrient in one serving—not the overall quality of the food.

faq.question: What should I look at first on a Nutrition Facts label?
faq.answer: Serving size. Every calorie and nutrient number is tied to that serving, so eating two servings usually doubles the listed amounts.

faq.question: What is the difference between Total Sugars and Added Sugars?
faq.answer: Total Sugars includes naturally occurring plus added sugars. Added Sugars is the subset added during processing or used as sweeteners.

faq.question: What does 20% Daily Value mean?
faq.answer: FDA uses 20% DV or more per serving as a general marker that a food is high in that nutrient; 5% DV or less is low.
